finalText:
Based on my research, I now have comprehensive information about both status codes. Let me compile the answer with proper evidence.

## Answer

HTTP status codes 301 (Moved Permanently) and 308 (Permanent Redirect) are both used to indicate permanent redirects, but they differ significantly in how they handle request methods and request bodies.

**Meaning:**
Both 301 and 308 indicate that the target resource has been permanently assigned a new URI and future references to the resource should use the new URI (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). The fundamental semantic difference is in how clients should handle the original request when following the redirect.

**Request Method Handling:**
The critical distinction lies in request method preservation. With a 301 response, a user agent may change the request method from POST to GET for the subsequent request for historical reasons (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). In contrast, 308 does not allow changing the request method from POST to GET—it preserves the original method (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html). RFC 9110 explicitly notes that 307 and 308 were added as "method-preserving redirects" to provide unambiguous semantics (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html).

**Request Body Handling:**
When a client receives a 301 and changes the request method to GET, the request body is not sent with the subsequent request. This is because RFC 9110 specifies that when the request method is changed to GET or HEAD, "remove content-specific header fields, including (but not limited to) Content-Encoding, Content-Language, Content-Location, Content-Type, Content-Length, Digest, Last-Modified" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). With 308, since the method is preserved, the original request body would be preserved and resent with the redirect request.

**Cacheability:**
Both 301 and 308 are heuristically cacheable by default. RFC 9110 lists both in its examples of "status codes that are defined as heuristically cacheable (e.g., 200, 203, 204, 206, 300, 301, 308, 404, 405, 410, 414, and 501 in this specification)" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). RFC 7538 specifies that "A 308 response is cacheable by default; i.e., unless otherwise indicated by the method definition or explicit cache controls" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html).

**Current Specification Locations:**
The 301 status code is currently specified in RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics (Section 15.4.2), which is the current HTTP semantics standard that supersedes RFC 7231 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). The 308 status code was originally defined in RFC 7538: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol Status Code 308 (Permanent Redirect) published in April 2015, and is also referenced in RFC 9110 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html).
